conditions_and_inference_limits.observation: Concentrated load applied to an unsupported center column, shear-tab center connections, exterior true-pin connections at beam mid-height. TN1749 uses chord length1.89m (6.21ft). The same beams were reused in all nine tests, with beam-web doubler plates to prevent bearing deformations around beam-web holes. This is not by itself a sudden dynamic column-removal test or nine wholly independent new assemblies.

Footnote4 defines chord length as horizontal distance between bolt centerlines at the ends; span length is distinguished as distance between column centerlines. TN geometry specifies 19mm A325 shear-tab bolts,32mm A490 exterior bolts, threads excluded from shear planes,9.5mm shear tabs,38.1mm horizontal centerline-to-edge distance and shear-tab depths229/305/381mm for3/4/5 bolts.

Tensile-test data for the steel components were not provided; representative stress-strain curves and failure strains were used with calibration referenced to Section3.1.1. Detailed models place bolts initially centered in standard holes and assume zero initial tension. These are model statements, not independently verified original test pretension or measured stress-strain data.

conditions_and_inference_limits.classification: later model choice informed by comparison
conditions_and_inference_limits.observation: Reduced models include an initial zero-load axial gap to1.6mm in tension and compression, said to yield better agreement than neglecting it; that gap is not applied in the vertical-shear spring law. Only half the assembly is modeled with symmetry conditions.

An exterior pin gap element also represents1.6mm slippage. Bolt springs use147kN ultimate capacity and failure displacement1.15 times displacement at ultimate load, based on predicted bolt shear. Calculated tensile bearing capacity is159kN and compression/tension yield capacities111/98.5kN. These are model-law values and not original individual test measurements.

Measured beam axial force plotted is an average of the two spans. TN1749 reports three tests per size; measurements for5-bolt test1 are not presented because initial data were missing. Table means and COVs do not separately declare the constituent test IDs.

TN1749 says its rotations are about5percent larger than Thompson's, using1.89m between bolt centerlines instead of Thompson's reported1.99m exterior-pin-to-center-column-face distance. Preserve both conventions; no rotation conversion has been calculated for this transcription.

Both models predict bolt-shear fracture in every case, while experiments reportedly include bolt shear, shear-tab tensile rupture and shear-tab block shear. Computed peak load always corresponds to initial failure, but experiment4-bolt test1 and5-bolt test3 have their peak at a secondary failure. Peak comparison therefore does not automatically compare identical failure stages.

Axial-force agreement is reported weaker than vertical-load agreement; forces are sensitive to axial restraints and gaps. An alternative study used axial springs to represent unknown test-frame stiffness; TN1749 instead uses connection gaps. No original measured test-frame stiffness is supplied on these pages.

Reduced-model quadratic unloading without permanent offset was selected over initial-stiffness linear unloading because it gave better agreement with measurements. Thus these displayed comparisons are not wholly unused holdout tests for all choices. Figure3-21 shows both vertical load and axial force, with beam-chord rotation and center-column displacement axes; no curves were digitized.

Section3.4 concentrates deformation in connections and treats beam spans as rigid bodies with negligible bending/axial deformation. Its beam chord rotation is arctan(displacement/chord length). This is an analytical convention, not authorization to silently overwrite original reported rotations.
